note: Source says rules that "may" in some measure make amends; candidate asserts "will".
replacement: With this aim, he first described to his neighbors the horror of a situation that armed every man against the rest, made their possessions as burdensome to them as their wants, and offered no safety either in riches or in poverty. Then he easily devised plausible arguments to bring them round to his design. "Let us join together," he said, "to protect the weak from oppression, to hold the ambitious in check, and to secure for every man what belongs to him. Let us set up rules of justice and peace, which all without exception may be bound to obey. These rules may make up in some measure for the caprices of fortune, by subjecting the powerful and the weak alike to reciprocal obligations. In a word, instead of turning our forces against ourselves, let us gather them into a supreme power that will govern us by wise laws, protect and defend all the members of the association, drive off our common enemies, and maintain eternal harmony among us."

note: Latin "ipso facto" was translated; style note keeps Latin as served.
replacement: I know that some writers have given other accounts of the origin of political societies, such as the conquest of the powerful or the association of the weak. It makes no difference to my argument which of these causes we choose. Still, the one I have just laid down appears to me the most natural, for the following reasons. First, in the case of conquest, the right of conquest is no right in itself, so it could not serve as a foundation for any other. The victor and the vanquished remained in a state of war toward each other, unless the vanquished were restored to the full possession of their liberty and freely chose the victor as their chief. Until then, whatever capitulation had been made was founded on violence and therefore ipso facto void. On this hypothesis, there could have been neither a real society or body politic nor any law other than that of the strongest. Second, in the case of the association of the weak, the words strong and weak are ambiguous. In the interval between the establishment of a right of property, or prior occupancy, and that of political government, the meaning of these words is better expressed by the terms rich and poor. For before laws existed, men had no other way of subjecting their equals than by attacking their goods or by handing over some of their own goods to them. Third, the poor had nothing to lose but their freedom. It would have been utterly absurd for them to give up voluntarily the only good they still enjoyed, and to get nothing in exchange. The rich, on the other hand, had feelings, if I may so express myself, in every part of their possessions. It was therefore much easier to harm them, and more necessary for them to take precautions against harm. In short, it is more reasonable to suppose that a thing was invented by those it would serve than by those it must have harmed.

note: The conditional "if the magistrate ... has a right" became a flat assertion that he has the right.
replacement: If we reflect on this subject with even a little attention, we shall find new arguments to confirm this truth, and we shall be convinced from the very nature of the contract that it cannot be irrevocable. Suppose there were no superior power capable of ensuring the fidelity of the contracting parties or of compelling them to perform their reciprocal engagements. Then the parties would be sole judges in their own cause, and each would always have a right to renounce the contract as soon as he found that the other had violated its terms, or that they no longer suited his convenience. It is on this principle that the right of abdication may possibly be founded. Now, if we consider here only what is human in this institution, it is certain that, if the magistrate, who has all the power in his own hands and appropriates to himself all the advantages of the contract, has none the less a right to renounce his authority, the people, who suffer for all the faults of their chief, must have a much better right to renounce their dependence. But the terrible and innumerable quarrels and disorders that would necessarily arise from so dangerous a privilege show, more than anything else, how much human governments needed a more solid basis than mere reason. They show how expedient it was for the public tranquillity that the divine will should step in to invest the sovereign authority with a sacred and inviolable character, which might deprive subjects of the fatal right of disposing of it. If the world had received no other advantages from religion, this would be enough to impose on men the duty of adopting and cultivating it, abuses and all, since it has saved more blood than fanaticism has ever spilled. But let us follow the thread of our hypothesis.
